chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Suleiman ibn Khalid, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man with whom wealth of mine was held, so he contended with me over it and swore an oath. Then wealth of his came to be with me; should I take it in place of my wealth that he took, and dispute it and swear upon it, just as he did? He (peace be upon him) said: 'If he betrayed you, do not betray him, and do not enter into what you blamed him for.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on taking back a debt from someone who falsely swore to withhold it, should I also swear falsely to take it?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between legal right (*haqq*) and ethical conduct (*akhlaq*), ruling that while one may legally seize the debtor's wealth, one must avoid the specific sin of *jahd* (withholding or denying) and false swearing that characterized the debtor's initial breach. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on *ihsan* (excellence in conduct), where a believer refrains from mirroring the oppressor's moral flaws even when exercising their due rights, thereby preserving spiritual purity over mere transactional justice.
